title: Polynomial-time approximation of EFX
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Determine \(\alpha _{\mathrm{alg}} = \sup\){\(\alpha \in [0,1]\) : there is a deterministic algorithm that, on every finite instance of nonnegative rational additive goods, returns a complete \(\alpha -\mathrm{EFX}\) allocation in time polynomial in the binary input length}. The number of agents is unbounded and part of the input.
why: Separates the efficiently attainable fairness guarantee from the purely existential EFX frontier.

progress.text: A polynomial algorithm achieves the universal factor \((\sqrt{5}- 1)/2\).
The survey retains the gap beyond this general EFX approximation and distinguishes exact existence from computation.
A preprint improves the \(2/3-\mathrm{EFX}\) guarantee to eight agents, while retaining about 0.618 as the known general frontier.

definitions: An instance has \(n\ge 1\) agents, \(m\ge 0\) goods and an explicit table of values \(v_{i},g=p_{i},g/q_{i},g\), with integers \(p_{i},g\ge 0\) and \(q_{i},g>0\) in binary. Its bit length N includes n, m and the table. For \(S\subseteq [m], v_{i}(S)=\sum _{g\in S}v_{i},g\). An allocation \((A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n})\) partitions \([m]\) into labeled bundles, possibly empty; its output lists one owner for each good. It is \(\alpha -\mathrm{EFX}\) if \(v_{i}(A_{i})\ge \alpha \cdot v_{i}(A_{j}\setminus \{g\})\) for every pair i,j and every \(g\in A_{j}\), including goods worth zero to i. All comparisons use i’s values. Empty \(A_{j}\) imposes no inequality; a singleton leaves value zero. Each fixed \(\alpha\) in the set must have one finite, always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants C,k with runtime at most \(C(N+1)^{k}\) on every instance. The machine, C and k may depend on \(\alpha\), but not on n, m or the valuations. \(\alpha\) is a fixed guarantee, not an input; no polynomial dependence on an accuracy parameter is required. The supremum is the least upper bound of these achievable factors; attainment at the endpoint is not assumed. The set is nonempty since \(\alpha =0\) is trivial, and is bounded by 1 by definition.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \alpha _{\mathrm{alg}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any additional complexity assumption must remain explicit and yields only a conditional bound.

context_blocks.title: How to read the approximation factor
context_blocks.text: Higher \(\alpha\) means a stronger guarantee, with \(\alpha =1\) giving exact EFX. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods of another bundle at 5 and 1. For this pair, the restrictive removal leaves value 5, so the inequality holds exactly when \(\alpha \le 4/5\). This illustrates one pair’s test, not a lower bound for every allocation of an instance.

context_blocks.title: The known general guarantee
context_blocks.text: Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos give a polynomial-time algorithm with factor \((\sqrt{5}- 1)/2\approx 0.618\). Their definition covers every good, even zero-valued ones. Thus the checked bounds are \((\sqrt{5}- 1)/2\le \alpha _{\mathrm{alg}}\le 1\); the upper endpoint here comes from the definition, not from an impossibility theorem.

context_blocks.title: Why the number of agents matters
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 preprint reports a \(2/3-\mathrm{EFX}\) algorithm for up to eight agents. This improves the guarantee on that restricted domain, while the present question requires a single algorithm for arbitrarily many agents. Its stronger-looking factors for EF2X and other k-good relaxations allow more removals and therefore do not give the same EFX guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Existence, computation and a supremum
context_blocks.text: TCS-1116 asks about universal existence without an efficiency requirement; this card additionally requires polynomial bit complexity. The 2023 survey treats the existence frontier and explains the known algorithmic guarantees. Even \(\alpha _{\mathrm{alg}}=1\) would not by itself provide an exact EFX algorithm: different algorithms might approach 1 without any attaining it. The word supremum deliberately preserves this distinction.

sentences: All indivisible goods must be allocated among agents with nonnegative additive values.
An \(\alpha -\mathrm{EFX}\) allocation lets each agent retain at least an \(\alpha\) fraction of the value she assigns to any other bundle after any one good is removed.
The question asks for the supremum factor guaranteed by deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for arbitrarily many agents.
A general factor of about 0.618 is known, while recent \(2/3\) guarantees cover only bounded numbers of agents.
The Lean benchmark accepts a certified determination with absolute error at most 0.01 throughout the stated numerical domain.
